pedagogy.summary: Two distinct ideas sit inside this topic and should be taught in order: (1) foods can be grouped by the NUTRIENT they mainly provide and each nutrient has a job — carbohydrates for energy, proteins for growth and repair, fats for energy/warmth and storage, and vitamins, minerals, fibre and water for keeping the body working and protected; and (2) a BALANCED diet means the right AMOUNTS from each group, not just having them all. Children readily learn the nutrient-jobs but the balance/proportion idea is the harder, more important one — it is why 'eat lots of everything' or 'fat is bad' are wrong. Bridge the science framing (nutrient groups) with the everyday UK Eatwell model (food-on-the-plate proportions: fruit/veg and starchy carbs biggest, protein and dairy smaller, oils/spreads tiny, sugary/fatty treats outside and occasional). Teach with real/pictured foods the child eats, classify them, then BUILD a balanced plate so proportion is something they construct, not a rule they recite. Note many foods (pizza, sandwich) are mixtures — a subtlety worth surfacing.
bestPractices: Teach nutrient→job first with familiar example foods (bread=energy, chicken=growth, etc.), then move to the harder idea of BALANCE — right amounts from each group.

Use the Eatwell 'build a plate' proportion model so balance is constructed and seen, not memorised: fruit/veg and starchy foods largest, protein and dairy smaller, oils/spreads small, treats outside and occasional.
Classify real or pictured everyday foods into groups, and explicitly handle MIXED foods (a sandwich, pizza) so children see foods aren't always one group.
Correct 'good food / bad food' thinking: no single food is banned; it's the overall balance and amount over a day or week that matters (per NHS guidance).
Avoid over-precision — no calorie counting; keep to groups, jobs and rough proportions appropriate to age, and connect diet to energy for activity and materials for growth.
keyRepresentations: Nutrient→job table with example foods (carbs=energy, protein=growth/repair, fats=energy/warmth, vitamins/minerals=protection, fibre=digestion, water=hydration)
Eatwell-style plate showing the five food-on-the-plate groups by proportion
A 'build a balanced plate' sorting surface where portions fill each segment
Sorting bins for classifying everyday foods (and a 'mixed foods' bin for pizza/sandwiches)
commonMisconceptions: 'Fat (or carbs, or sugar) is bad and should be avoided' — missing that fats/carbs are needed for energy; it's balance and amount that matter.
'A balanced diet means eating a bit of everything equally' — missing that the PROPORTIONS differ (more fruit/veg and starchy food, less oil).
'Foods belong to exactly one group' — many everyday foods (pizza, sandwiches, milk) are mixtures.
'Vitamins/minerals give you energy' — they protect and help the body work; energy comes mainly from carbohydrates and fats.
'Healthy food = salad only / treats are forbidden' — rather than occasional treats fitting within an overall balance.
'You must eat perfectly at every meal' — missing that balance is judged over a day or week.
'Protein is only meat' — missing beans, pulses, eggs, dairy and fish as protein sources.

learn.summary: Teach two ideas in order for ages 7–9: (1) foods can be grouped by the main nutrient they provide and each nutrient has a job (carbohydrates for energy; proteins for growth and repair; fats for energy, warmth and storage; vitamins, minerals, fibre and water for keeping the body working and protected); and (2) a balanced diet means the RIGHT AMOUNTS from each group, not just having a bit of everything. The nutrient→job layer is easier; the proportion/balance idea is the harder, more valuable one and explains why 'eat lots of everything' and 'fat is bad' are wrong. Bridge the science framing to the UK Eatwell Guide (which replaced the earlier Eatwell plate in 2016: fruit/veg and starchy carbs biggest, protein and dairy smaller, oils/spreads tiny, sugary/fatty treats outside and occasional), build balanced plates by hand rather than reciting rules, surface that many foods (pizza, sandwiches, milk) are mixtures, and frame balance over a day or week rather than per-meal perfection. Avoid calorie counting; keep to groups, jobs and rough proportions.

activities.title: Build a balanced plate
feedback: If the plate is all one food, ask: which nutrient jobs are now missing — where is the energy, the growth material, the protection? Point back to the empty segments.
If portions are equal across all groups, prompt: the Eatwell Guide makes fruit/veg and starchy foods the biggest parts and oils/spreads tiny — adjust the amounts, not just which foods are present.
If a treat is placed into a main group, note that high fat/sugar foods sit outside the main groups and are eaten less often.
Praise correct reasoning that names the nutrient's job, not just that a food 'is healthy'.
activities.rationale: Constructing and adjusting proportions makes the abstract ratio of a balanced diet concrete and lets children discover, rather than memorise, that amounts differ by group. Building a plate matches the Eatwell proportion model and the curriculum requirement to reason about the right types AND amount of nutrition.
sourceClaims: The Eatwell Guide divides foods into five main groups — fruit and vegetables and starchy carbohydrates (each just over a third of the plate), protein foods, dairy and alternatives, and oils/spreads (small amounts) — with high fat/salt/sugar foods outside the main groups, eaten less often; balance is judged over a day or week, not every meal.
Y3 pupils should identify that animals, including humans, need the right types and amount of nutrition, and that they cannot make their own food; they get nutrition from what they eat.
learnerActions: Collect real or pictured everyday foods the child actually eats, then sort each by the main food/nutrient group it belongs to (starchy carbohydrates, protein, dairy/alternatives, fruit/veg, oils/fats, treats).

Arrange foods onto a plate divided into Eatwell proportions so fruit/veg and starchy foods fill the largest areas, protein and dairy fill smaller areas, oils/spreads fill a tiny area, and sugary/fatty treats sit off to the side as occasional.
Deliberately try an unbalanced plate — a mountain of chips only, or nothing but fruit — and describe what is missing and which nutrient jobs are not covered.
Say what each food's nutrient does (e.g. bread = energy, chicken = growth and repair) as it is placed.
Look across a whole day or week and check whether one wobbly meal is evened out by the others.
activities.intendedInsight: Balance is not 'a bit of everything equally' — it is the right amounts, with fruit/veg and starchy foods making up most of the plate and treats only occasional; and balance is judged over a day or week, not at every single meal.

activities.title: Match each nutrient to its job
feedback: If a learner says vitamins give energy or build muscle, separate the jobs: energy comes from carbohydrates, growth from protein; vitamins keep the body working and protect it, but are not fuel.
If protein is named only as meat, broaden to eggs, beans, lentils, fish and dairy — the nutrient does the job, not one specific food.
If energy is attributed only to sweets, distinguish quick sugar from the sustained energy of starchy carbohydrates.
activities.rationale: Establishing nutrient→job with familiar foods gives learners the vocabulary and functional reasoning they need before tackling proportion, and directly targets the common 'vitamins give energy' and 'protein = meat only' misconceptions. The specific nutrient functions are an age-appropriate framing not stated verbatim by the cited sources.
learnerActions: Reveal, one group at a time, what each nutrient group does for the body and list example foods: carbohydrates = energy; protein = growth and repair; fats = energy, warmth and storage; vitamins and minerals = protection and keeping the body working; fibre = digestion; water = hydration.
For each group, predict and then check what might happen if you ate too much or too little of it.
Name at least five groups with an example food for each, and explain the job of carbohydrates, proteins and fats in your own words.
activities.intendedInsight: Each nutrient does a distinct job; vitamins and minerals protect and help the body work but do NOT supply energy — energy comes mainly from carbohydrates and fats.

activities.title: Sort mixed foods
feedback: If a sandwich is forced into a single group, ask what the bread, filling and spread each contribute.
Confirm when a learner correctly identifies milk as a mixture: it belongs to the dairy group and also supplies protein, fats and minerals such as calcium.
activities.rationale: Explicitly handling mixed foods prevents the 'foods belong to exactly one group' misconception and makes real-world classification honest. This is a sound teaching proposal not directly evidenced by the cited sources.
learnerActions: Classify everyday foods into nutrient-group bins, including a dedicated 'mixed foods' bin.
Break down mixed foods — a pizza, a sandwich, a glass of milk — into the groups they contain, naming each part.
Discuss why one food can belong to more than one group.
activities.intendedInsight: Many real foods are mixtures of several groups, so classifying whole meals is not always one-to-one.

activities.title: Myth-busting: is this food bad for me?
feedback: If a learner says fat should be avoided completely, explain the body needs some fat for energy, warmth and storage; the issue is amount and balance, not cutting out a whole nutrient.
If a learner endorses Sam's oranges/vitamin-tablet plan, point out vitamins don't supply energy or build muscle — identify the carbohydrate source for energy and the protein source for growth.
If treats are called forbidden, reframe: occasional treats can fit within an overall balance.
Reward answers that reject 'healthy = strong' reasoning and correctly assign carbohydrates to energy and protein to growth.
activities.rationale: Discussion is well suited to confronting value-laden 'good food/bad food' thinking and the 'fat is bad' and 'vitamins give energy' misconceptions; it may complement, rather than replace, the hands-on plate building where proportion is best constructed. The Eatwell claim supports the 'no food banned / eaten less often / balance over a day or week' principle this activity rests on.
sourceClaims: The Eatwell Guide divides foods into five main groups — fruit and vegetables and starchy carbohydrates (each just over a third of the plate), protein foods, dairy and alternatives, and oils/spreads (small amounts) — with high fat/salt/sugar foods outside the main groups, eaten less often; balance is judged over a day or week, not every meal.
learnerActions: Pose 'is X bad for me?' questions and answer using nutrient jobs and overall balance rather than a 'good food / bad food' verdict.

Consider Sam's claim that fat is always bad and should be avoided completely — explain why the body still needs some fat (for energy, warmth and storage) and that it is the amount and balance that matter, not banning a whole nutrient.

Work through the swimmer example: Sam says he'll eat lots of oranges and take vitamin tablets because 'vitamins give you energy and make you strong' — decide whether to agree and explain what he should eat for energy (carbohydrates: bread, pasta, rice) and for building muscle (protein: chicken, fish, eggs, beans), and why each helps.
Reason about what might go wrong on race day if someone ate only protein and no carbohydrates, and why we still need vitamins regularly in our food even though they give no energy.
activities.intendedInsight: No single food or nutrient is simply 'bad' or 'banned' — even fats are needed for energy, warmth and storage; it is the overall balance and amount across a day or week that matters, and each nutrient must be matched to the job it actually does.

constraints: Teach nutrient→job first with familiar foods, then move to the harder balance/proportion idea.
Do not introduce calorie counting; keep to groups, jobs and rough age-appropriate proportions.
Correct 'good food / bad food' thinking: no food or nutrient is banned, including fat; overall balance and amount over a day or week is what matters.
Classification tasks must explicitly include mixed foods (pizza, sandwich, milk) so learners do not assume one food = one group.

Recognition/matching tasks (categorising foods, picking the balanced plate) consolidate and assess but do not by themselves require learners to construct and adjust proportions — pair them with hands-on plate building.
A tap-to-reveal or lift-the-flap plate teaches the nutrient→job layer well but does not let the learner construct and adjust proportions; treat it as a scaffold toward building a plate.

Optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete: dragging foods into segments that fill up, a balance gauge that visibly tips when a tray is overloaded, instant group-classification feedback, and a day/week view showing a single wobbly meal evening out. These are illustrative, not mandatory.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original source listed a 3D format as 'poor' with the claim '3D adds no conceptual value'; this universal comparative claim is not established by the cited sources and has been dropped rather than propagated as a pedagogical law.

The original 'ideal' rationale asserted that building proportions is something 'no static image or quiz can do'; this comparative necessity claim is not supported by the cited sources. It has been softened to a narrowly scoped affordance (construction/adjustment) plus an objective limit (recognition tasks don't elicit independent construction).

sourceClaims were narrowed to [] on the 'Match each nutrient to its job' and 'Sort mixed foods' activities: the curriculum claim is a general necessity assertion that does not state nutrient functions, and no cited claim establishes the nutrient→job mapping or the mixed-foods principle. Those contents are retained as sound, age-appropriate proposals, not as source-evidenced findings. The build-a-plate activity retains the curriculum claim because it specifically references the right 'amount' of nutrition, which maps to the proportion/balance principle; this is a borderline rather than clear-cut support.

The 'fat is always bad' probe question from the original assessment had been dropped from the candidate's learner-facing activities despite being a prominent misconception; it has been restored to the myth-busting activity with matching feedback.

The diagnostic 'correctAnswer' states vitamins do not 'directly build muscle'; this is consistent with the age-appropriate framing (energy from carbohydrates/fats, growth from protein) and no error was found. Framing fats as 'warmth and storage' is simplified but acceptable for ages 7–9.

Source claims cite the Eatwell Guide and the national curriculum; they support the teaching principles of proportion and 'right types and amount of nutrition' but do not constitute evidence that any specific activity here was tested for effectiveness.

probeDeeper: Sam says fat is always bad and should be avoided completely. Is there any reason the body needs some fat?
If Sam ate only protein and no carbohydrates at all, what might go wrong on race day?
If vitamins don't give energy, why do we still need them every day?
assess.correctAnswer: Disagree with Sam. Vitamins don't give energy or directly build muscle — they help the body work properly and protect it from illness. For energy he needs carbohydrates (bread, pasta, rice); for building and repairing muscle he needs protein (chicken, fish, eggs, beans). What matters is the JOB each nutrient does, not whether a food merely seems 'healthy'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Vitamins give you energy and build muscle ('oranges make you strong').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the jobs: energy comes from carbohydrates, growth from protein; vitamins keep the body working and protect it — useful, but not fuel. Sort foods by the job they do.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — oranges and vitamin tablets give energy and build muscle, so Sam's plan is good.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Endorses Sam's plan; names vitamins as the energy or muscle source.

errorPatterns.pattern: Energy only comes from sugary or sweet foods ('eat sweets for energy').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish quick sugar from the sustained energy of starchy carbohydrates; connect to what athletes actually eat before endurance events.
errorPatterns.distractor: He should eat sweets and sugary drinks for energy.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Recommends sugary foods/drinks as the energy source rather than carbohydrates.

errorPatterns.pattern: Only meat builds muscle, so you can't build muscle without eating meat.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Broaden protein sources beyond meat (eggs, beans, lentils, fish, dairy); the nutrient, not the specific food, does the job.
errorPatterns.distractor: Only meat can build muscle, so Sam must eat meat.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names meat as the sole protein source; excludes eggs, fish, beans, dairy.

responseLevels.gap: Judges foods only as 'healthy' or 'unhealthy', or thinks vitamins give energy; can't match a nutrient to its job.
responseLevels.full: Matches each nutrient to its function AND reasons about a real diet — why carbohydrates fuel the race, protein builds muscle, vitamins protect without giving energy — and can say what fails if a group is missing.
responseLevels.partial: Names food groups with examples and can recite carbs=energy, protein=growth, but treats them as a list — can't reason about whether a particular diet meets a specific need, or slips on vitamins.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Sam is training for a swimming race and wants stronger muscles. He says 'I'll eat lots of oranges and take vitamin tablets, because vitamins give you energy and make you strong.' Do you agree with Sam's plan? What SHOULD he eat for energy and for building muscle — and why does each food help with its job?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks 'healthy = strong/energy' or 'vitamins give energy' endorses Sam. A child who understands nutrient function rejects the plan and correctly assigns carbohydrates to energy and protein to growth. Because the tier-two 'why' forces the nutrient-to-job link, you can't land it by guessing that oranges are healthy.
